summary:
GravityGuard (G2) is a crew health monitoring system for long missions, where Earth is too far away to watch astronauts in real time. We built a working web app with two sides. On board, astronauts see their vitals compared to their own preflight baseline, and G2 flags slow changes that persist for days, such as a rising resting heart rate or declining strength and balance. On Earth, a flight surgeon reviews those records after they arrive over a simulated delayed, encrypted link and sends feedback back to the crew.

This addresses the challenge by moving health monitoring onto the spacecraft. Emergency warnings run on fixed rules, not AI, so they work offline and never wait for a reply from Earth. An optional AI medical assistant explains health questions using the astronaut’s own data and a curated library of NIH and NASA references. We also designed a smartwatch interface concept for at-a-glance alerts.

This matters because on the way to Mars, a message can take up to 22 minutes each way. Bone and muscle loss happen slowly, so crews need a tool that catches gradual trends early and keeps a doctor in the loop despite the delay.
details:
What it does and how it works

GravityGuard (G2) is a crew health monitoring system for missions too far from Earth for doctors to watch in real time. Astronauts use an onboard dashboard and a virtual G2 smartwatch. Together they track heart rate, blood oxygen, heart rate variability, strength, balance, sleep, steps and symptoms. G2 compares each reading to that astronaut’s own preflight baseline and flags changes that hold for days, such as resting heart rate up 15% or strength down 8%. The watch also catches short-term warning signs right away, like blood oxygen dropping below 92% on two readings in a row. Records go into an encrypted queue and reach Earth over a simulated delayed link that can also drop out. A flight surgeon sees each record only after it arrives, reviews it and sends feedback back up. An optional AI medical assistant answers health questions using the astronaut’s relevant data and cites a curated library of NIH and NASA references.

Benefits and intended impact

Astronauts get an early, private view of their own health trends. Urgent symptoms escalate immediately on board, without waiting for Earth. Flight surgeons get clean records that show when each one was captured and when it arrived. The goal is to support Earth-independent crew care for the Moon and Mars. The same baseline-tracking idea could also help people on Earth in remote or bed-rest care.

Tools and technologies

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite and Recharts.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and SQLite, with SQLite FTS5 for searching the reference library.

Security: Fernet encryption for the message queue, and passwords hashed with PBKDF2.

AI: Meta’s Muse Wonder model, optional and off by default.

Testing: 185 automated backend tests (pytest) and browser tests (Playwright).

Hardware: none. The G2 watch runs in the browser with six built-in test scenarios (normal, poor sleep, exercise recovery, a concerning trend, and others). A real smartwatch can plug into the same data format later.

What makes it creative

Most health apps assume an instant connection. G2 is built around delay: it works fully offline and syncs only when the link allows. We split safety from AI on purpose. Emergency warnings run on fixed rules and never wait on a model, while the AI only explains. We also added a Real Research Data Replay mode. It plays back 481 real heart-rate readings from a public PhysioNet dataset to show the pipeline handles real measurements. That data is clearly labeled as Earth ICU data and kept fully separate from astronaut records.

Factors we considered

Communication delays of up to 22 minutes each way at Mars.

Slow bone and muscle loss that single checkups miss.

Never letting AI diagnose: alerts say “cause not established, review recommended.”

Labeling every simulated reading as simulated, and keeping each astronaut’s records private from the rest of the crew.
dataRefs: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
